article.title: DeepSeek Harness Team Open-Sources a Super-agent Prototype That Finds and Fixes Bugs on Its Own

blocks.text: The DeepSeek Harness team on the evening of October 31 published a design write-up on what it calls a Super-agent, an always-on agent that pushes several tasks forward at once, looks for work on its own and recovers from faults, and released a companion research prototype on GitHub under the MIT license, Chinese tech media reported.

The repository, dsh-superagent-prototype, packages a proactive coding agent for a single GitHub repository as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness. It listens to GitHub and, optionally, Feishu. When an allowed user asks for work, it opens a work item, handles it in its own session and directory, and replies in the original conversation, for example with a pull request. The README stresses that this is research code rather than an official DeepSeek product, and that some designs in the write-up are not implemented.

The core idea is a two-layer architecture. A resident Router session takes in all human interaction across channels and only dispatches tasks; it does not do the work itself and may not even have a Bash tool. Isolated Worker sessions run tasks concurrently with full tools and report back to the Router instead of talking to users. Each Worker subscribes to the threads it cares about, such as a pull request or a chat topic, so follow-up events go straight to it without passing through the Router.

The system is event-driven: chat messages, emails, review comments and CI results arrive as triggers, filtered first by deterministic code and then by a model. The team also separates agent state from execution environments so the agent can stay online in the cloud while reaching a user's own machines, and runs an external Watchdog session that checks whether Workers are making real progress. In the team's internal user group, an instance follows a rule to silently reproduce reported bugs and speak up only once it has a simple fix, sometimes opening a pull request before anyone has tagged it.

In preliminary tests on synthetic workloads of about 300 messages with roughly 20 work requests, the Super-agent finished half of tasks within 12.4 minutes and 95% within 15.7 minutes, ahead of a single session with a subagent tool, at the cost of more cached tokens. Without direct routing of follow-ups to Workers, Router decisions rose by about 30%, and batching under load lowered the inference time per Router decision from 6.4 seconds to 1.6 seconds. The team called the results a preliminary reference.
Open problems it lists include scaling the Router, long-term memory, agent-to-agent communication, and prompt-injection risk when a cloud agent can reach credentials on local devices.
